text: I will be staying on the board of directors, and will remain on as CEO to deliver our first event in the Middle East, Web Summit Qatar, at the end of February which is looking to be double the size we expected. (P.S., You should come: https://t.co/gfs7HSOFiJ!)

Sadly, it does mean I’ll be stepping down as Web Summit CEO on March 1. I’ve absolutely loved my time with Web Summit. I’ve been bowled over by the team's talent, energy, and frankly -- general good vibes -- and this appreciation has only grown with each passing week.
My first day is March 25th! Unreal.

NPR represents so much of what I believe in: the importance of civic institutions, high-quality public information, and our universal human inclination to curiosity. I couldn’t be more excited to join this incredible institution and essential mission. 🎉

Big news: I’m delighted to announce that I will be taking up the position of CEO of NPR starting in late March. NPR has been a lifelong part of my soundscape, and I credit its reporting with sparking my curiosity that set me onto the path to become the person I am today.

I am not from a global majority country, but have done a decent amount of work in that context, and agree with you how important that experience is.

Okay last gripe. WHAT IS THE DIFFERENCE between a remote workforce and a large corporation with many offices. Answer: we zoom from our bedrooms. Anyone who has worked in a company with multiple locations knows that someone somewhere is always remote to you.

Don’t get me wrong. I’m an office person! When I had the choice of working from home versus going to the office, I went in probably 95% of the time. But I ran a remote organization and this sort of grumbling is a failure of empathy and imagination.

And the line about quick answers to questions when one can stroll to a desk kind of belies that point. Office work is ALL interruptions, all the time. Also, the author appears to be unfamiliar with Slack and the myriad other ways of summoning attention.

The argument that working from home has greater distractions than an in office job is clearly written by someone accustomed to the luxury of a dedicated office with a door that shuts and a personal assistant gatekeeping your calendar

I particularly like the entirely speculative and gratuitous hand wave about SVB potentially failing because *the employees were working from home* rather than because the CEO lobbied to lift regulatory supervision or the execs and board failed to adequately supervise risk.

Users want delight and discovery, advertisers want safety and predictability, governments want oversight and control. How one walks those line is what constitutes success, not protocols or grand philosophies.

There are a few different ways to get there in terms of content moderation and T&S models, and you could argue Twitter could use some innovation in this regard, but ultimately the constraints are pretty fixed.

The challenge is exactly as described. The best platforms in terms of user value (and hence, revenue value) are not wild free for alls, they are deeply curated spaces of curious delight and overall safety.

There will always exist for me an alternative, where our response wasn’t to invade an unrelated nation, or to go shopping, but to console our communities, to provide resources to the suffering, to honor their legacy with healing rather than vengeance.

We talk about the wars and politics, but we don’t talk enough about the trauma - of those deployed over and over, of Muslim American communities surveilled and stigmatized, of the pain and suffering of Iraqis and Afghan civilians, of the survivors, and of those who survived them.

I hate the legacy of that day, politically, geopolitically. I was 18 in my first days of college. My past 20 years were an unconscious response, working for human rights and civil liberties in the Middle East and at home. It’s only recently I realized I had a home front, too.

Right after he passed, my mom told me that the day the towers fell, she couldn’t stop being panicked that she had lost him. And she had. It took twenty years for her to get the phone call, but eventually it came.

I can’t imagine how much undiagnosed trauma there has been in the greater tri-state area in the past 20 years; how many people like my dad left us years before their time as a result of the psychological wounds of that day. It doesn’t feel right.

For all that exists for survivors, it turned out there were almost no resources available to someone with the mental wounds he carried. I spoke to many genuinely kind caseworkers, who all told me they only dealt with physical illness, and told me to talk to my elected officials.

He died this past year of complications from alcoholism, a condition brought about at least in part by his intense PTSD. We found all his 9/11 paperwork, and it fell to me to call around to the NYC and national 9/11 registries to report his death.

My dad was a 9/11 survivor, a fact he was never comfortable with. For him, he wasn’t in the towers, and he walked out of downtown that day. But in the logic of the aftermath, both physical and mental, that was enough to recognize him as part of the 9/11 registry.

There’s a whole interesting conversation about lesser meatlessness, like eating fish or chicken, or eggs and dairy. But like all things, I believe in moderation in moderation. Absolutism gets us nowhere, and even just restoring meat to being special is a great place to start.

For most of these 25 years I’ve been lukewarm on meat alternatives - why be ersatz? But over the last few years, they’ve really come leaps and bounds. But I still prefer to use them as complementary to a meatless diet, not a direct translation.
(I highly recommend Levantine/Persian/Turkish/Georgian/Armenian food for meatlessness.  Pretty much anything eastern Mediterranean through the Black Sea!) https://t.co/gCGvseloPe

As more people opt into meatlessness, options expand! My favorite Guamanian spot in SF went from being primarily porky (obviously) to really expanding its meatless repertoire. The smoked eggplant situation is 🤤 with spectacular flavor and nuance.

But most cuisines also have robust meatless repertoires; after all, most people couldn’t afford special all the time. Plants and grains are the workhorses of our diets. We just haven’t spent as much time refining our understanding of what they bring to the table.

Our understanding of most cuisines has been shaped by what’s in restaurants and what we eat with family for special occasions. Because meat was expensive, it was often what was special. We hold meat at the center of cuisine as a result.

I recognize there are some people who have cultural connections deeply tied to meat. How do I forgo lumpia or goat stew or bratwurst? This is an interesting question! Forgoing those is a choice, but it doesn’t mean turning your back on a cuisine.

I see the meat-free life is having a day! Come on in, the water is warm! I’ve been opting out for 25+ years and friends often still forget when meal planning and restaurant picking. To me, that’s the best evidence that one can be completely meatless without undue disruption.

And, my passion: we created a global, multilingual, sprawling consultation with thousands of contributors that led us to set a strategic direction for @Wikimedia by 2030: The essential support system for free knowledge. And anyone, anywhere, who shares our vision can join us.

We rolled out award-winning mobile apps and experiences, including a @Wikipedia app on KaiOS, one of the most popular operating systems in South Asia and Africa. Oh yeah, and we updated @Wikipedia on the desktop for the first time in 12 years! But not too much. Just enough. 😂

We waged campaigns for human rights and free knowledge across the globe. We litigated and advocated our way to overturn of a 2.5 year block of @Wikipedia in Turkey, and we stood up with the @UNHumanRights to increase the quality of human rights information available online.
We launched a Universal Code of Conduct to elevate contributor conduct and stop harassment on our sites. Harassment has no place in free knowledge or on @Wikipedia. Ever. https://t.co/dMfw6OIbFT

We raised more than $500 million for free knowledge over 5 years, built an endowment, and gave out tens of millions in grants to communities around the globe. This spring, we launched a dedicated $4.5 million fund for Knowledge Equity, which I expect to see continue to grow.

Our community presence in Africa, specifically sub-Saharan Africa, grew by 500 percent since 2014, measured by the number of organized @Wikimedia volunteer affiliates. 🌍 Did you know 40% of the world's population will be African by 2100?
We increased women editors to @Wikipedia by more than 30 percent in the last year, driven by new contributors from Africa, the Americas (both Latin America and Northern America), and Oceania.

The @Wikimedia movement grew from a collection of communities and chapters to an aligned, powerful, passionate global social movement for knowledge, justice, and social change, with more than 100 organizations around the world.

We invested in shoring up trust, confidence, and our usefulness in places where everyone knows and loves @Wikipedia. And then we looked to the future: Africa, Asia, Latin America, the Middle East. We built community and software for the future of free knowledge.
Under my watch, we reversed our traffic decline, and grew reader engagement by 30%. We also reversed our contributor decline, growing editorship by 36%. Key to this? Emerging markets.

This brilliant, vivacious man succumbed to a disease that tormented him and us, and stole the love of my mom’s life. We lost my dad to two of the greatest American tragedies of my lifetime. And his is just one story. Everyone has one, this year. https://t.co/x6QBzKr3w0

And it was COVID. And also 9/11. He had been downtown just blocks away when the planes hit and the towers fell, locked in an office as the sky turned black. He suffered from PTSD, and his drinking went right to the races.

It was internal bleeding in the end, unchecked C diff from a recent hospital stay, but his death certificate also says alcoholism. That comforts me. Too much of the misery of addiction is hidden for shame. It should not be shameful, but it is brutally painful.
He died alone. The first responders found him. They wouldn’t let us see him.

I went home to San Francisco, I’d been gone for three months and I needed to be back in my own life. My mom called a week later, said he’d gone silent again. Should she call 911? A wellness check? We agreed she would.

One day, we didn’t hear from him, he wasn’t answering calls. My mom was terrified, went to check on him. He was too weak to get out of bed, he’d lost his phone. She tidied everything, tucked him in. We told him to go to the hospital. He called 911 in the middle of the night.

I went home to the east coast for the summer to be there for my mom, working from the kitchen table. He moved back out. No more motels, we got him an apartment nearby. The drinking got worse. I extended my trip.

I was almost optimistic. Perhaps his increasing age and his community would slow him down, keep him afloat. But the world shut down, and the meetings went to zoom calls, it wasn’t enough. The telltale signs came back: the mug, the droopy lip, unexplained errands.

He had his longest period of sobriety ever when the pandemic hit. As his children, we’d resigned ourselves to the idea that his alcoholism was terminal, but he’d actually been doing well. He was in an outpatient program, he was back at home. He was going to meetings every day.

Living in San Francisco, every time I saw a homeless man of a certain age, I thought of my father. There but for the grace of god, but really, the grace of my mom. 40 years of marriage. She saw him clearly and she loved him all the same. She always believed there was a way back. https://t.co/uxIy6i3UCh

The past few years were really bad. We hid his car keys, he lived in recovery houses when things were good and cheap motels when they were not. He was a regular at the local ER, and a frequent inpatient for detox sessions. They saw him coming.

Again, he was incredibly generous and kind when he was sober. A volunteer mentor, an inveterate hugger. It’s just that the sobriety was as unpredictable as drinking. No way of planning for it, much of life was just waiting for the shoe to drop. https://t.co/zV9rZwYXix

It was 20 years of nerve-grinding uncertainty and gaslighting. Would he blow up over dinner? What was that in the coffee mug? How quickly could we exit him from a party? Any effort to address his drinking, while he was drinking, brought down a hail of verbal abuse.

My relationship with my dad was as much a relationship with his disease as anything. When he was sober, he was generous, loving, and adored by friends and the community. When he was drinking, he was unpredictable, cruel. A relationship with alcoholism is an abusive relationship.

My dad died in October, and I consider his death to have been caused by the pandemic, though he never had COVID. An alcoholic in unstable recovery, he lost his precarious hold on sobriety in the spring, and drank himself to death, alone, four months ago. https://t.co/PbXYzQa3Ib

We’re going to get it wrong more than right. But of all institutions, non-profits have a special obligation to do the work. Our orgs, founded in aspiration, often have all the same institutional problems as the societies we seek to change. The work starts at home.

This isn’t simple. It requires meeting the bravery of those who come forward with commensurate institutional courage. That’s not a solo act. It requires us all to step forward in unison. There is so much weight, legacy, and power that holds us back.

I regret that we failed to steward @SunFoundation forward. My closing hope is that failure is not received as a lesson. Organizations must grapple with their legacies of exclusion, toxicity, and harassment. Funders should support the work. Boards must be accountable and engaged.

We wanted this to be a turnaround story. We did not want the lesson to be "sweep it under the rug." We wanted it to be, "grapple with and own your legacy." We wanted this important organization to be able to openly reckon with a troubled past, and move forward with purpose.

I remain in awe of the bravery of the women, particularly @SarahSchacht, and others who came forward to speak out about the toxicity, exclusion, and harm that they and others endured. We owe you so much more. Thank you.

Make no mistake, @SunFoundation had a tremendous and positive impact on sectoral innovation for technology and transparency. It also had a corrosive and lasting impact on the professional and personal well-being of many people. Both things can be true.

I am disappointed we were not able to do more for @SunFoundation, and the people who loved it for what it could be, despite what it had been. When we closed down, it was staffed by many fantastic humans who truly believed in the mission and work. We will see them do so much more.

There were many reasons that we were not able to fulfill the vision that @zoe_reiter and I had for a thorough accounting of the past. That's for another time. But it's clear that those reasons are why so many organizations fail their people, particularly the least empowered.

I know @zoe_reiter and I are proud that we were able to release that review as part of our commitments. But there's no getting around it: we lost time and trust, and the opportunity to do the necessary restorative justice work that @SunFoundation would have required to thrive.

We regrouped. We hired the excellent Katherine Kimpel of Ramona Strategies, who undertook a thoughtful and uncompromising review, based on what she and her colleagues were able to ascertain.  https://t.co/9kWSujre9i

It turned out we were unprepared for this work. As only two volunteer board members, we had almost no capacity to handle the intake of former employee and community experiences on our own, in a systematized and substantive way. https://t.co/9FogoJ631b

As new directors to the board, in the midst of the #MeToo moment, @zoe_reiter and I felt that it was essential the organization reckon with its past. We worked together as allies and published our public plan as a first measure of accountability. https://t.co/7hYzNg0QhI

I distinctly remember being warned to watch out for advances. I took it to heart and stayed far away. I was afraid of what it would mean as a woman to have anything sexual, consensual or otherwise, linked to my professional reputation. I imagine most women know what I mean.

I was appalled by the account. But I also was not surprised. As a young woman in DC, the "community" of tech for transparency, civics, etc. had an alcohol-fueled social scene, and its most celebrated stars were often young men who could do no wrong.

In 2018, I was asked by @JohnWonderlich to join a renewed board, alongside @zoe_reiter, as part of a turnaround effort. Weeks later, the Huffington Post released an account of alleged sexual misconduct and mistreatment by a former Sunlight employee. https://t.co/JOVNdBJOmb

I never worked directly with @SunFoundation. But I went to their panels, read their blogs, used their tools, admired their teams. When I heard they were shutting down in 2016, I signed my name to an open letter objecting to the decision, worried about the loss to the community.

The @SunFoundation ended a nearly 15-year run this week. I was on the board of directors that made the decision that it was time to close the organization.

@sharmine_04 We really appreciate that you are a part of what makes free knowledge possible. Wikipedia belongs to the world, and I hope you are proud too!

@sharmine_04 We ask because we know many people are happy to support this important resource for their own use and for the good of their community. We hear from donors that they are proud to be a part of making it possible.

@sharmine_04 Having said all this, I also really do understand people who feel like it’s not fair to ask people with unequal economic circumstances to donate. We will always be free. We will *never* make *anyone* to pay to access Wikipedia.
@sharmine_04 But these aren’t what we use day-to-day. They are saved away for a “rainy day” and we can only access them in exceptional circumstances.

@sharmine_04 Finally, our reserve and assets are a lot, and we are fortunate. We’ve been planning for a long time to make sure we have resources to keep Wikipedia going even through a major economic crisis, because it’s a critical resource that the world can’t afford to lose.

@sharmine_04 We think it’s important that about 10% of the annual budget goes to this creative, organic community work, with community committee review. Community volunteer editors are the people who make Wikipedia possible.

@sharmine_04 Our grant budget goes to support the work of community groups around the world. Anyone who wants to improve or add to Wikipedia can apply for a grant. They can use it to take photos to upload to articles, or to present on research about women in technology, for example.

@sharmine_04 We also see how much salary inflation affects income inequality, particularly executive pay. We maintain a ratio of about 8:1 for our compensation range, instead of 100s:1 for big companies. We don’t believe in paying huge amounts to execs, instead we want to pay fairly to all.

@sharmine_04 We know that salaries vary across the world. We to be fair employers because we are hiring in very competitive industries (software engineering!). At the same time, we are a non-profit. We make an effort to pay right at the middle of the market. No special bonuses or benefits.

@sharmine_04 We have more than 250 people who work just on these problems. It sounds like a lot, but compared to most major websites, it’s a very small team! And the cost of maintaining this engineering capacity is the most expensive part of our budget — not hosting costs.

@sharmine_04 We also have to make this possible on as many operating systems, devices, and processing power setups as possible, from a dial-up modem in an Internet cafe to an iPhone on 5G. This requires a lot of attention to detail.

@sharmine_04 Similarly, our ability to support 20+ Indic languages along with 250+ other languages is thanks to our great engineers, researchers, and designers. We support roughly 6 times as many languages as the average “global” website (300 vs 50).

@sharmine_04 For example, while hosting costs have stayed relatively low as a percentage of our budget, that’s because of the work of our engineers on issues like redundancy, reliability, security, and speed.

@sharmine_04 Hi there, and thank you for your donation! I read the thread and understand why you’d be concerned based on how it is written. However, I don’t think it quite captures the complexity of the global work that we support, and how it compares to other websites of this size.

It’s everyone's responsibility to do everything in their power to prevent further harm. At @Wikimedia we're taking these steps to protect our communities, colleagues, and families, while keeping @Wikipedia thriving. We’re asking you to join us in keeping people safe. 🌍 (12/13)

Through it all, we're focused on keeping @Wikipedia up and the world informed. We're supporting our volunteers around the world who are working diligently to curb misinformation and provide quality, comprehensive articles about the pandemic. 🦠 ↓ (11/13) https://t.co/fshHzgTkbt

We’re looking at how to respond to the broader moment. Our product teams are working with our community members to find ways to better showcase information about coronavirus, including designs for how to host essential info on Wikipedia’s front page. 📰 (10/13)

We’re working to lighten the load and focus on only essential work. Our SRE teams have to keep Wikipedia up, our HR and finance folks have to keep payroll flowing. 50% time only works if we deprioritize non-essential work. So we’re doing that. 💻(9/13)
We're not tracking our colleagues' time. People will work when they can, and when they can’t, we trust they’ll be right. 🙏 (8/13)

We’ve also instituted a 50% work requirement. We’re only asking for 20 hours a week. We know many people do more for our mission, but we want to be supportive of those who can’t, for reasons such as childcare, illness, or their own mental health. 🤲(7/13)

Now, all staff are fully remote. And we're instituting measures to reduce their cognitive strain so people can stay healthy and care for loved ones. We’ve waived the use of sick days or PTO for COVID-19 related care. ❤️ (6/13)

We took COVID-19 seriously early on. Seventy percent of our staff already work remotely. But, when we learned of community transmission in the Bay Area two weeks ago, we mobilized all staff to work from home. Within 24 hours, our San Francisco and DC offices were closed.⏱️(5/13)

@luis_in_brief YES. Started reading but have gotten sidetracked. Let’s do it.
Yes, the North, yes all of us, yes America. Yes, our original collective sin and unpaid debt. Yes, reparations. Yes, on this day.

I think about this often. I think about it when I go home and see a pineapple door knocker on a New England saltbox. I think about it when I consider my Irish immigrant ancestors entering a society built on slavery capital. I think about it anytime people say, not the North.
It goes on. If there was a way to profit off of slavery while also keeping it at a proper, deniable remove, New England did it. $$$

Not to mention that a goodly portion of the local Native American population was enslaved, for #reasons or no reason at all, and sent down to the islands to labor. Most perished. Colonialists made money. $$$

All those prim New England families with their pineapples as symbols of hospitality, brought as exotic offerings from the Caribbean? 🍍Spiky fruit catching a ride back from tending to the plantations, purchased with funds from the trade. $$$

Capital for industrialization came from somewhere: 17th-century CDOs. Buying, shipping, and sustaining people as a commodity was expensive, so people devised fancy financial instruments. Enslaved humans, the original asset backed finance offering. Oh hey, banking industry. $$$
That famed cod of the Cape? The fishing industry packaged it and sent it, rank and rotting, to feed enslaved Africans. $$$
The difference being that the plantations were off-shored, to the Caribbean.

Not only did New England yes have the legal institution of slavery, albeit briefly, quite a bit of the economy of New England, including my home coast of Connecticut, was built on the backs of plantation labor.
Man, were my fourth grade history classes misrepresenting some things.

(I referred to it as my summer reading broccoli book, as in, it was good for me. Everyone should read broccoli books! This year’s was The Warmth if Other Suns by Isabel Wilkerson, which was hefty but fantastically readable. Like broccoli with Velveeta.)

I grew up feeling superior (hah, how white of me) because I was from New England and my part of the country didn’t have slaves, or so I’d been taught.

Anyway, I love my job, I love the mission, I love the Wikimedia community - with all our flaws and imperfections, and commitment to constant improvement. Just always feel the need for healthy caveats on the nature of power in Wikimedia.
Because those principles come from the volunteer community, I’m also accountable to the community. So the power and the accountability both reside in them, and what they have built.

When you operate with such clear guiding principles, it does make the role itself powerful, because it allows us to declare for what we believe and devote resources accordingly. It also allows us stand firm and speak without equivocation against violations of those principles.

The thing Wikimedia volunteers share are common values and a belief in the power of free knowledge to improve the state of the world. That is itself a powerful belief, with a good deal of moral clarity.

Wikimedia is powerful because of the volunteer community who makes it possible. They would no sooner take direction from me than anyone else. I am an imperfect steward for something built by millions of people, all with their own views and experiences.

At the same time, those very same attributes of the work always make it funny for me when I hear that I “run” Wikimedia or am “powerful” in some sort of way. My role certainly entails a lot of responsibility, but has very little hierarchical power or control.

... gaining a breadth of perspective on various countries, cultures, and communities, working without positional authority - all these experiences inform my work every single day at Wikimedia. No CS degree required.

Co-building solutions, devolving control to the margins, enabling and supporting emergent properties and features, paring technical solutions down to the bare minimum for effective and sustainable functioning (open really does some heavy lifting here)...

But it was tech second, outcomes first. Every day we were challenges to find the simplest, most resilient and most sustainable solutions to challenges, be they reducing HIV/AIDS transmission or cultivating more responsive local government.

I used my knowledge of and affinity for tech, particularly new trends in mobile networking in emerging economies, and a love of free culture, to shove a foot in the door of the world of international development. And that’s where I started to thrive.

I didn’t get accepted to any of the universities I wanted to go to. I moved to Cairo, Egypt, instead. I pursued BA in Middle Eastern and Islamic Studies, got fired from my first job as a banker (which I always hated), and it was only then my tech love came back into play.

I want to role model that you don’t have the be a dude with a CS degree to run a tech organization. In fact, I’d argue you might be better off and much better suited with a different background. My geeky love of technology was a background factor on my journey.
